narrative:
The model predicted a 55% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 26 was the strongest influence; it sits well below the average of 37 among accepted students and strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your family income being in the High bracket was the second most important factor. This actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing, since very few accepted students come from high-income families. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.8 was the third key factor. It fell noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the outcome toward failure.

Taken together, the lower LSAT and GPA outweighed the positive effect of your family background, resulting in the rejection.

What you should do next is clear: focus on raising your LSAT score. Retake the test, invest in quality preparation, and aim for a result closer to or above 37. Once that improves, reapply. Your high family income and full-time study plan are already working in your favor; strengthening the LSAT is the single change most likely to flip a future prediction from fail to pass.
